captions.instagram:
What is Ohm's law?

Twice the push, twice the flow: one line of algebra runs every heater, charger and fuse in your home. Drive electrons round a 3D circuit, see why they crawl while the light comes on instantly, and find where Ohm's law finally breaks.

→ Ohm’s law: current equals voltage divided by resistance. Double the push, double the flow.
→ Squeeze the flow with more resistance and the current falls. The line on the chart gets flatter.
→ A heater is just a resistance: a 1,500 W air fryer element is about 35 ohms.
→ A car starter pulls about 150 amps. On a thin cable, the wire itself becomes a heater.
→ Switch on too much and the current climbs past 16 amps. The MCB’s strip bends and trips.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/ohmslawclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.description:
Twice the push, twice the flow: one line of algebra runs every heater, charger and fuse in your home. Drive electrons round a 3D circuit, see why they crawl while the light comes on instantly, and find where Ohm's law finally breaks.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/ohmslawclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/ohmslawclear

In this video:
• Voltage pushes, resistance holds back. Current is how much charge flows each second.
• Resistance turns electricity into heat. The heat made each second is P = I² × R, or V² ÷ R.
• Low voltage needs fat cables. For the same power, a 12 V battery must push twenty times the current of a 230 V socket.
• MCBs guard wires, RCCBs guard you. Too many heaters on one circuit push the current past 16 A and an MCB trips to save the wire.
• Where the straight line bends. A bulb filament's resistance rises about 14 times as it heats, so it surges at switch-on.
